html:
The oligarchic coup of 411 BCE overthrew the democracy of Athens and put a council called the Four Hundred in power. It lasted only about four months.

The disaster of the Sicilian Expedition had left Athens short of ships and money. Rich Athenians who had long disliked rule by the many saw their chance. Alcibiades, then living with a Persian governor, hinted that the Persian king would fund Athens if it gave up democracy. Leaders such as Peisander, the orator Antiphon and Theramenes used threats and murders to push the Assembly into voting power to the Four Hundred, with a promise of a wider body of five thousand citizens later.

The plan broke on the navy. The fleet at Samos, rowed by poor citizens, refused to accept the new government, declared itself the true Athens and called Alcibiades back. The Four Hundred split, Euboea revolted, and they fell. A mixed regime of the Five Thousand followed, and full democracy returned in 410 BCE. Antiphon was tried and executed. Oligarchy came back once more under the Thirty Tyrants in 404 BCE.
sum: The oligarchic coup of 411 BCE overthrew the democracy of Athens and put a council called the Four Hundred in power. It lasted only about four months.
